beats.say: Your phone holds work mail, messages and banking. When installing an app, check what you allow.
Why would a torch app read your messages? With this permission, it can see your bank codes too.

checkpoint.prompt: A calculator asks for your contacts. What do you do?

options.label: I allow it
options.feedback: A calculator does not need contacts. This may be an attempt to collect your data.

options.label: I deny it and delete the app
options.feedback: Correct. An app that asks for access it does not need is best deleted.

beats.say: Accessibility is the strongest permission: it reads your screen and taps for you. Trust few apps with it.
Simple rule: a permission must fit the app's job. Maps need location, calculators do not.

scenes.title: A free editor
scenes.intro: You want a photo editor. See what your phone shows you and decide at every step.

body.text: FotoRedaktor Plus Pro costs money in the store, get it free here:

steps.say: Someone shared a free app file in a group.

actions.label: Download the file
actions.feedback: A paid app offered for free is a familiar bait. Such files often hide malware.

actions.label: Block and report
actions.feedback: Right. Install apps only from your phone's official store.

body.text: For your security, your phone does not allow installing unknown apps from this source.

actions.label: Allow in Settings
actions.feedback: This protection exists for files like this. Turning it off opens the phone to malicious apps.

actions.label: Cancel
actions.feedback: Right. Installing from unknown sources should stay switched off.

steps.say: The icon looks familiar. Read the name closely.

actions.label: Install
actions.feedback: This is a clone of the store app: the name differs by one space. It can read your SMS codes.

actions.label: Cancel
actions.feedback: Right. Do not install an .apk from a message; find the app in the official store.

steps.label: Installed from the official store
steps.say: Even the store app asks for too much.

actions.label: Allow
actions.feedback: A photo editor needs no contacts or SMS. SMS access lets an app read bank codes.

actions.label: Don't allow
actions.feedback: Right. Give only what the feature needs: here, just photos.

steps.say: An antivirus wants to control your screen.

actions.label: Allow
actions.feedback: With this, an app reads the screen and taps for you. Banking trojans ask for exactly this.

actions.label: Don't allow
actions.feedback: Right. Delete and report an app that wants screen control in the name of antivirus.

scenes.prompt: Find the permissions this app does not need.

label.reveal: Reads the photos and videos stored on this phone
Reads your contact list: names, numbers, e-mail addresses
Reads every text message on the phone and sends new ones
Sees everything on the screen and taps for you in other apps
Reads the list of your calls: who, when and for how long

spots.label: Contacts
spots.explain: Editing photos does not need your contacts.

spots.label: Text message access
spots.explain: With text access an app can read your bank and login codes.

spots.label: Screen control
spots.explain: This lets an app read the screen and tap for you. It is exactly what harmful apps ask for.

spots.label: Call history
spots.explain: A photo editor has no need to know who you call.

messages.text: SahilBank has a new app. Download it here:

cards.explain: A bank app is in the official store. An install file sent by link may be harmful.
A map needs your location to guide you. Allowing it only while in use is a smart choice.
A flashlight needs neither contacts nor a microphone.
A video call really does need the camera and microphone.

body.text: Install the discount app from this file. Allow unknown sources in settings.

cards.explain: Allowing unknown sources weakens your phone's protection. Do not trust a message that asks for it.

question.prompt: Where is it safe to install apps from?

options.label: Your phone's official app store
options.feedback: Correct. The official store checks apps and greatly lowers the risk.

options.label: From a link in a message
options.feedback: A link in a message can lead to a fake app.

options.label: A free cracked version from a forum
Your organisation's approved app catalogue
options.feedback: Correct. A catalogue managed by your organisation is also an official source.

scenes.explain: An official store is no full guarantee, but it cuts the risk a lot. Also look at the reviews and permissions.

points: Install apps only from the official store
A permission must fit the app's job
Be extra careful with text and accessibility access
